As a specialized corporate vehicle within the Veralogix Group, Veramani must navigate a multifaceted regulatory landscape governed primarily by the Companies Act 71 of 2008, the King IV Report on Corporate Governance, and the stringent tax directives of the South African Revenue Service (SARS) [cite: 1, 2, 3].

## 1. The Standard CIPC Registration Framework for IT Holding Entities

The most prevalent CIPC (Companies and Intellectual Property Commission) structure for an IT holding group in South Africa is the Private Company, designated as a Proprietary Limited or "(Pty) Ltd." [cite: 4, 5]. This registration requires the submission of a Notice of Incorporation (CoR14.1) and a Memorandum of Incorporation (MOI), which serves as the foundational governance document [cite: 4, 6]. For a holding entity that does not trade independently, the MOI must be meticulously drafted to empower the board to exercise control over its subsidiaries through both equity ownership and management intervention [cite: 5, 7].

### CIPC Registration and Compliance Requirements

| Compliance Pillar | Requirement Details | Statutory Basis |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Company Type | Private Company (Pty) Ltd | Companies Act S14 [cite: 4] |
| MOI Status | Customized to allow investment and management focus | Companies Act S15 [cite: 7] |
| Director Mandate | Minimum of one South African resident director | Companies Act S66 [cite: 4] |
| Beneficial Ownership | Mandatory filing of ultimate natural person owners | General Laws Amendment Act 22 [cite: 8] |
| Annual Returns | Filed within 30 business days of the anniversary date | Companies Act S33 [cite: 4] |

Recent legislative amendments, specifically the General Laws Amendment Act 22 of 2022, have introduced a rigorous Beneficial Ownership (BO) transparency regime [cite: 8]. Veramani is legally obligated to maintain a Beneficial Interest Register that identifies any natural person holding a 5% or greater stake in the company, whether that stake is held directly or through intermediary corporate veils [cite: 5, 8]. This requirement is critical for maintaining compliance in the wake of South Africa's FATF greylisting, as failure to disclose ultimate human owners can lead to criminal prosecution under Section 214 of the Companies Act [cite: 8].
